definition: Learners take up or reject structured reasoning supports depending on whether those supports are perceived as usable, relevant, and worth the effort in the learning situation.
description: This cluster captures the learner-side response to reasoning aids, examples, feedback, and virtual cases: some supports are adopted and processed, while others are ignored, judged too complex, or seen as offering limited added value. In the realist logic, the mechanism is the learner’s appraisal and use of the offered structure or feedback, which can lead to improved diagnostic estimation, recognition of missing information, repeated correct answers, or illness-script development when the resource is taken up. Where the support feels time-consuming, overly complex, or insufficiently useful, the response is non-use or only limited learning.

definition: Instructional resources that prompt learners to compare confusable cases, organise features, and combine analytic with similarity-based reasoning to improve diagnostic accuracy.
description: This cluster represents a family of teaching resources that structure diagnosis around contrasts: compare-and-contrast prompts, differential tables, feature-oriented instructions, paired examples, and guided combined-strategy practice. In realist terms, these resources work by offering a schema for noticing shared and distinguishing features, which can reorganise knowledge and shift learners toward more structured, combined reasoning; in novices this is associated with improved performance and greater accuracy after contrastive learning. The cluster also includes resources that can create confusion when combined instructions are too dense, showing that the mechanism depends on how the instructional input is framed and used.

definition: A set of teaching and case-design resources that structure learners’ diagnostic reasoning by prompting hypothesis generation, modelling expert thought, and guiding checking and practice around clinical cases.
description: This cluster represents interventions that make clinical reasoning visible and actionable: students are prompted to query an initial hypothesis, compare it with contradictory or absent findings, and practice reasoning in individual, small-group, seminar, or course-based formats. The resources include explicit modelling/explanation of expert reasoning, teacher-led consultation, video-enriched or virtual patient cases, and bias-focused prompts such as search-satisficing instruction and self-monitoring. In realist terms, these interventions offer structured cues and practice opportunities that can trigger learners to think during hypothesis query, understand physician thought processes, and refine or correct diagnoses.

definition: Learners respond to structured examples, prompts, reflection, and practice by organizing and storing diagnostic knowledge into more coherent illness-script and disease-mechanism structures.
description: This cluster captures a mechanism-response in which learners move from poorly developed illness scripts and weak links to disease mechanisms toward more structured diagnostic knowledge. Worked examples, case-based reflection, self-explanation, and embedded prompts appear to support selective organisation, storage and retrieval of knowledge, detection of misunderstandings, and proposed illness-script enrichment, often with lower cognitive load and greater confidence. The same response can also be seen in delayed-test gains and improved MCQ performance, especially when learners engage diligently with practice and feedback.

definition: Learners respond to time pressure, competing demands, and repeated case exposure by forming faster, more secure case representations and relying on implicit recognition rather than explicit theoretical understanding.
description: This cluster captures a response pattern in which learners confronted with simulated ward multitasking, short case windows, multiplied patient encounters, and competing pager demands move toward quicker recognition and more secure case representations. Across the studies, the offered resources include varied cases, case-based diagnosis/explanation, and theory-provided tutorials or games, but the learner response is often frustration, limited perceived benefit from theory, or no discernable difference in approach. The mechanism is the shift from deliberate theoretical processing to implicit learning and faster recognition under pressure, especially for students near transition to junior doctor.

definition: Learner reasoning that proceeds without explicit strategy support, often as simple diagnosis or spontaneous/analytic responding to cases and features.
description: This cluster captures a response pattern in which learners are left to diagnose, notice features, or reason spontaneously with little or no explicit learning process guidance. Across the studies, this shows up as minimal exposure, speeded single-diagnosis work, natural-strategy or spontaneous-reasoning instruction, and unguided practice with biasing or incorrect suggestions; the common outcome is weaker or less effective implementation, shorter engagement, missed self-explanation, and lower accuracy. In realist terms, the mechanism-response is the learner’s unguided diagnostic processing, which is especially visible when novices or low-support conditions lead them to rely on whatever strategy they already have rather than a newly scaffolded one.

description: This cluster represents a mechanism-response pattern in which learners are given prompts, explicit cognitive-feature focus, or guided consultation steps and then respond by generating explanations, thinking more actively, and keeping their reasoning on track. definition: A pattern of diagnostic performance in which learners show fewer miss errors and greater resistance to misleading information despite limited gains in underlying biomedical understanding.
description: This cluster describes an outcome where learners become less likely to miss the correct diagnosis or be led astray by misleading information, even though their pathophysiology knowledge and deep conceptual understanding do not substantially improve. It appears in settings with difficult far-transfer cases, worked examples containing errors plus KCR feedback, and official diagnosis feedback after each case, alongside unsupported similar-case reasoning with reduced feedback. In realist terms, the offered resources and case demands seem to produce a more error-resistant diagnostic response, while leaving the deeper knowledge base largely unchanged.
